claims.text: An active-learning machine-learning surrogate trained on a sparse set of ab initio molecular-dynamics data for both solid and liquid phases can predict fusion and high-temperature free energies efficiently and accurately.
The surrogate can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions to free energy.
A neural-network interatomic potential can capture the free energies and associated entropy terms of both solid and liquid states.
Active learning can selectively sample configurations from ab initio molecular dynamics and thereby reduce the number of expensive simulations required.
The initial application domain is elemental and binary systems near their melting points.
A trained machine-learning potential represents local atomic environments and vibrational dynamics.
Representing local environments and vibrational dynamics allows detailed electronic interactions to be translated into cheaper predictions of free-energy landscapes.
Learning the configurational features that control free energy allows the model to approximate expensive ab initio evaluations.
Active learning identifies high-uncertainty configurations that may contribute significantly to entropy or anharmonicity and resamples them.
Selective resampling of high-uncertainty configurations maintains accuracy while reducing computational cost.
Relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics, the proposed workflow will reduce computation time by roughly one order of magnitude.
The proposed workflow will have fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics for phase free energies and thermodynamic observables.
The proposed workflow will outperform TOR-TILD for systems beyond binary compositions.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD are highly accurate but computationally intensive, especially for multicomponent systems.
Effectiveness beyond binary systems remains to be established.
Rare or extreme configurations may limit the model's ability to capture electron–vibration coupling and anharmonicity in multicomponent systems.
Aluminum and Fe-C near melting are proposed as elemental and binary benchmark systems, respectively.
The method is considered successful only if it achieves at least a tenfold cost reduction while keeping phase free energies and derived observables within a 10% error margin.

contradictions.description: The boundary says the approach is already 'experimentally validated initially' for elemental and binary systems, whereas the conditions and benchmark design describe that validation as future testing. No evidence record documents prior validation.
